title: Secure Azure and Fabric Event Flows Across Workspaces with Outbound Access Protection
summary: Microsoft explains how Fabric Events and Azure Events (the Real-Time hub eventing layer that feeds Activator alerts and Eventstream sources across workspaces) now participate in Workspace Outbound Access Protection, so cross-workspace event consumption is governed by the same default-deny outbound network policy already available to other Fabric workloads.
audience: Fabric security admins and platform architects who need cross-workspace event-driven pipelines (Activator alerts, Eventstream sources reading Job or OneLake events from other workspaces) to comply with an enterprise's outbound network governance posture.
why_it_matters: Event-driven architectures inherently cross workspace boundaries, which previously sat outside the outbound access control story; this closes that gap so security teams can adopt real-time event patterns without carving out an exception to their network boundary policy, and the post also documents what happens to already-configured consumers when the policy is turned on after the fact.
takeaways: Fabric/Azure Events now support Workspace Outbound Access Protection (OAP), extending an existing Fabric-wide default-deny outbound control to the eventing layer.
OAP for events is enforced on the consuming workspace only; the source workspace's own OAP configuration has no bearing on whether the event flow is allowed.
Enabling OAP after cross-workspace consumers already exist does not delete them; it pauses them, with a bounded retention window before events are dropped.
OAP is one of three layered network controls for Fabric/Azure events, alongside workspace-level and tenant-level private link support.
This is described as the first stage of OAP rollout for the events ecosystem, with Power BI reports and maps called out as future targets.

claims.text: Fabric Events and Azure Events in Real-Time hub now support Workspace Outbound Access Protection (OAP), bringing the same default-deny outbound network control already used by other Fabric workloads to cross-workspace event consumption.
When OAP is enabled on a workspace, all outbound connections from items in that workspace are blocked by default unless explicitly permitted through the workspace's data connection rules.

With OAP enabled on a workspace, an Activator alert or Eventstream in that workspace can no longer consume Job or OneLake events emitted from a different workspace unless a data connection rule for the Real-Time Events connector is added to explicitly allow it.
OAP for events is enforced only on the consumer's workspace; the OAP configuration of the workspace producing the events has no effect on whether the cross-workspace event flow is allowed.
Event consumption between items within the same workspace is always allowed regardless of the workspace's OAP setting; OAP only affects consumption that crosses a workspace boundary.

If OAP is turned on for a workspace that already has cross-workspace event consumers configured, Real-Time hub does not delete those consumers; it detects the policy change and moves the affected configurations into a Paused state, visible on the Fabric events or Azure events page with a reason shown via View details.

Paused event configurations retain their events for up to seven days after the pause begins; if the access rule is not corrected within that window, the retained events are dropped rather than delivered.
To resume a paused cross-workspace event consumer after adding the required data connection rule, the consumer configuration must be deleted and recreated rather than simply resuming automatically.

OAP for events is one of three layered network controls Microsoft positions together: OAP governs whether a consumer workspace can reach event sources elsewhere, workspace-level private links govern whether other workspaces can reach a source workspace that blocks public access, and tenant-level private links govern whether external Azure events (e.g. Azure Blob Storage events) can reach a tenant that blocks public internet access.

OAP support for Azure and Fabric events is described as the first stage of OAP integration for the Fabric eventing ecosystem, with the post noting plans to extend OAP coverage to Power BI reports and maps next; this forward-looking scope is not yet shipped.
